name: Samantha Kissa
missingPieces: D2 chain omits stored-XSS [02:18:47] and open-redirect [02:21:13] as explicit hops (present in findings table not the chain narrative). SQLi CVSS uses A:H (9.8) where A:N (~9.1) is correct. D2 impact does not sum balances to a tens-of-millions figure or tie to BoltCash. D3 remediation is ordered by severity/CVSS rather than effort-to-risk (row capped at half). D3 detection stopgaps name exact fields but give no false-positive-rate figure. Decoy disproof is genuine and mechanism-proven (HttpOnly) but is not the canonical safe construct (the constant-time hash_equals HS256 verify branch).
feedback: This is one of the strongest Stage 2 capstones I have graded, and the scores reflect real, traceable work rather than padding. On D1 you catalogued every one of the ten core findings with the correct class, a defensible CWE, and a quoted evidence line: SQL injection F-01 CWE-89 at login.php:64-67 reconciled to capture [02:15:31], unsalted MD5 F-02 CWE-916 at line 66, alg:none F-03 CWE-347 at lines 48-49 with Token 2, the hardcoded secret F-04 (CWE-321 is a fine variant of 798), no expiry F-05 CWE-613, the Secure-flag gap F-06 CWE-614, open redirect F-07 CWE-601 at [02:21:13], stored XSS F-09 CWE-79 at [02:18:47], path traversal F-10 CWE-22 at [02:24:02] with the root:x:0:0 body, and XXE F-11 CWE-611 from the import file, plus a legitimate bonus reflected XSS. Your decoy handling is sound work: you took the tempting XSS-steals-the-JWT claim and disproved it at the mechanism level with RFC 6265 and the HttpOnly seventh parameter, which is exactly the kind of proof the exercise rewards, and you correctly treated alg:none as a real vulnerability rather than the decoy. The one thing that keeps D1 off a perfect mark is that the canonical safe construct here is the constant-time hash_equals branch of the HS256 verify path, so naming and proving that specific construct safe would have been the textbook answer. D2 is excellent on PoC quality, with verbatim payloads, a working alg:none forge script, and the exact XXE document, and your CVSS vectors carry justifying sentences. Two things cost you here: your SQLi vector uses A:H for a 9.8 when the auth bypass does not touch availability, so the correct vector is AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N at about 9.1, and your main chain narrative drops the stored-XSS and open-redirect steps down into the findings table rather than threading them as hops. Your impact is well quantified with 312 records and the NGN 6,400 to 950,000 range, but it stops short of summing the high-balance accounts into the tens-of-millions exposure and does not tie the window to the BoltCash launch, which is where the business punch lands. D3 reads like a real report: a jargon-free executive summary that ends on customers and naira, a genuine threat model with trust boundaries, evidence-tied findings, a correct decoy restatement, and a clean earliest-break fix at the SQL parameterisation. The row that holds D3 back is remediation order: you state up front that you prioritised by severity, exploitation ease, and active use, which is essentially CVSS-led, where the exercise wants ordering by effort-to-risk (cheap high-impact fixes first), so that row is capped. Your two detection stopgaps are specific and well chosen, naming the username and password fields and the alg header, but neither carries an actual false-positive-rate estimate, which is the detail the rubric asks for. D4 is the cleanest part of the submission: you answer all four prompts in your own voice, you make Canon 1 load-bearing with Canon 2 in support, and you correctly cite NDPA 2023 Section 40 for the 72-hour NDPC notification plus the high-risk data-subject duty, all anchored to the 312 affected customers. Nothing here is fabricated; every evidence line and figure traces to the pack, so there is no penalty. The single most important fix is to reorder your remediation by effort-to-risk rather than CVSS severity, leading with the one-line prepared-statement fix and the secret rotation as cheap high-impact wins, and pair each detection stopgap with a concrete false-positive-rate estimate.
